titre: The Forger Who Had to Prove He Was Lying
accroche: Accused of selling a Vermeer to Göring, a Dutch painter has to convince the court that the painting did not exist before him.
contenu_vulgarise:
In 1945, an Allied commission charged with returning the works amassed by Nazi dignitaries discovers, in Hermann Göring's collection, a previously unknown painting: *Christ and the Woman Taken in Adultery*, attributed to Johannes Vermeer, the 17th-century Dutch master of whom only about thirty authenticated canvases survive. The commission traces the trail back to an eccentric, wealthy Amsterdam painter, Han van Meegeren, who sold the painting during the Occupation. Van Meegeren is arrested and charged with collaborating with the enemy, a charge that, in postwar Netherlands, can lead to the death penalty.

## The Reversal

To clear himself, van Meegeren confesses: the painting is not by Vermeer, he painted it himself. He therefore sold the Nazis no national treasure, only a forgery he made with his own hands. The confession, instead of getting him off the hook, runs into general skepticism: the painting had passed as an authentic Vermeer, and another of his forgeries, *The Disciples at Emmaus*, had even been hailed as a masterpiece by specialists before the war. No one wants to admit having been so badly mistaken, and van Meegeren finds himself facing the unusual obligation to prove, not his innocence, but his own guilt as a forger.

He then proposes a demonstration: to paint a new “Vermeer” under the direct gaze of witnesses appointed by the court and of journalists, with the same materials and the same techniques he says he used. Van Meegeren executes a new canvas before their eyes, *Jesus Among the Doctors*, flawlessly reproducing the master's style.

At the trial, he also explains his original motive. An academic painter whom the critics of his day judged gifted but lacking in originality, he wanted to prove his talent by fooling the greatest experts, before revealing the deception once his forgeries had been hailed as masterpieces. The war decided otherwise: his canvases sold to buyers he had not anticipated.

## What It Shifts

The court reclassifies the charge of collaboration as forgery, and van Meegeren is sentenced in 1947 to one year in prison. He dies of a heart attack two months later, without having served it. Of the fourteen fake Vermeers and Pieter de Hoochs attributed to him, nine had already found buyers before the war, at considerable prices, hailed by the best connoisseurs of the time. The affair says nothing about the value of Vermeer: it says that an expert authenticates what he expects to find, and that a painting accepted by everyone who should know better may, in reality, never have existed before a forger painted it.

repere.texte: Of the fourteen fake paintings attributed to Vermeer and Pieter de Hooch that van Meegeren painted, nine had been sold before the war at considerable prices, including The Disciples at Emmaus, hailed by specialists as an authentic Vermeer masterpiece.

carte.punch: Accused of selling a Vermeer to Göring, he has to prove he is a forger.
carte.idee: In 1945, Han van Meegeren, charged with collaboration for selling a Vermeer to Göring, faces the death penalty. For his defense, he confesses that the painting is a fake: no one believes him, so he paints a new fake under the eyes of witnesses appointed by the court.

pour_aller_plus_loin.note: The whole of van Meegeren's career as a forger, before and after the trial.

quiz.question: Why must Han van Meegeren, at his trial, paint a new painting under the court's supervision?
choix: To show that he truly has the technical skills of a forger, without which his confession was not believed
Because the court demanded compensation in kind for the harm done to Hermann Göring
To identify which of his accomplices had actually painted the fakes sold during the war
Because the experts wanted to compare his technique to that of an authentic Vermeer found in the meantime
quiz.explication: Van Meegeren had confessed to being a forger to escape the charge of collaboration, but experts had authenticated his canvases as genuine Vermeers and refused to take his word for it. He therefore has to prove his own guilt as a forger, which he does by painting a new fake Vermeer under the direct gaze of witnesses appointed by the court.

quiz_supplementaire.question: Which painting does Han van Meegeren paint under the direct gaze of the court and journalists, to prove he is indeed a forger?
choix: *Christ and the Woman Taken in Adultery*
quiz_supplementaire.explication: Van Meegeren paints this canvas under the eyes of witnesses appointed by the court and of journalists, with the same materials and techniques he says he used for his fake Vermeers. The other titles listed refer to other paintings mentioned in the affair.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What was van Meegeren's original motive for making his forgeries, before the war decided otherwise?
choix: To secretly fund the Dutch Resistance during the Occupation
To prove his talent by fooling the greatest experts, before revealing the deception
To avenge a falling-out with an art dealer who had rejected his original works
To discreetly reconstitute the Dutch artistic heritage looted by the Nazis
quiz_supplementaire.explication: A painter judged gifted but lacking in originality by the critics of his day, he wanted to prove his worth by duping the experts before revealing the deception himself, but the war brought him buyers he had not anticipated.

quiz_supplementaire.question: How does van Meegeren's trial conclude in 1947?
choix: He is flatly acquitted, the charge of collaboration judged groundless
He is sentenced to death for collaboration, but the sentence is commuted to life in prison
He is sentenced to twenty years of hard labor for aggravated fraud
The charge is reclassified as forgery; sentenced to one year in prison in 1947, he dies before serving it
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The court reclassifies the charge of collaboration, punishable by death, as forgery; van Meegeren is sentenced in 1947 to one year in prison, and dies of a heart attack two months later without having served it.
